text: Every new workload in a hybrid, multi-cloud estate raises the same question: which cloud should this actually run on? Without a fixed order to answer it in, the same argument happens from scratch every time, with nobody checking the one thing that should end the debate immediately — can this even run where everyone's arguing it should.

So work it in order. First, the hard constraints from Chapter 6 — data residency and sovereignty — because they're non-negotiable and can eliminate an option before cost or preference ever enters the conversation. Second, check whether the workload's required services actually exist on each remaining candidate at all; this is a yes-or-no filter, not a scoring exercise. Only after both of those narrow the field do skill and cost become the deciding factors.

Take a workload built around one specific managed AI capability that only exists natively on one cloud. Run it through the filter: the cloud with that capability stays in, every other candidate is eliminated outright, regardless of what it would cost there or how well the team knows it. A workload built from portable building blocks instead — containers, generic VMs, object storage — survives this step on any candidate the compliance check already allowed.

Among whatever survives, skill and cost decide, and real effective cost at that — the organization's actual, discount-adjusted pricing from existing commitments, not a published list price that rarely reflects what either cloud would really cost this org. Landing a new workload on a platform the team doesn't operate well is a genuine risk independent of the invoice.

The honest default from Chapter 2 still holds: most new workloads belong on the cloud the organization already runs similar workloads on. Multi-cloud placement is a deliberate exception, chosen for a named reason, not a default applied just in case. That closes this chapter on cost and governance — next up is the capstone, designing a full hybrid and multi-cloud architecture end to end.
